title: Retainer or a fixed launch
excerpt: Fix the scope when you can describe the finished launch. Use a retainer when the product will keep changing and you want the same people on it.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf, a finished set with a clear edge.
caption: A small set, arranged and finished. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a design project be a fixed launch?
faqs.answer: Fix it when you can list the pages or screens and the sentence the site must say, and the work after launch will be occasional. Write what is out of scope. New ideas should be traded in writing, not quietly added.

faqs.question: When is a design retainer the better contract?
faqs.answer: Use a retainer when the product or the site will keep changing and you want the same people to make those changes. Name a capacity and keep a visible queue. If you cannot imagine a month of real work, you do not have a retainer yet.

faqs.question: What should a fixed launch hand over?
faqs.answer: Hand over the site in accounts you own, the files, and a short note on how to publish. Include a check you can point at, such as the form arriving in the right inbox. A launch you cannot edit is not finished.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
The choice in a design retainer vs fixed project is about whether the edge is visible. Fix the launch when you can describe the finished site or the finished version, and the work after that is occasional. Keep a retainer when the product or the site will keep changing and you want the same people in the room for those changes.

A retainer is not a friendlier way to buy a launch you could have scoped. A fixed project is not a way to freeze a product that is still finding its sentence. Match the contract to the motion.

## When the edge is clear

The edge is clear when you can list the pages, the states that matter, and the sentence the site must say. A marketing site for an offer you have already sold. A redesign of a shop whose catalog you understand. A set of screens for a flow you have watched people attempt. You can still be wrong about details. You are not wrong about the boundary.

Write the boundary in the scope. Pages or screens, the content you will provide, the things that are out: a second product, a brand film, a native app, an open-ended illustration series. The fixed project is a promise to cross that boundary and stop. Stopping is a feature. It lets you launch, learn, and decide later whether you need more.

Hanabi's work of this shape is a design-and-build engagement with a defined site or interface. The stack, when it is code, is Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, with Motion only where it helps, on Vercel. The point of naming the stack is that a fixed build can be finished. It is not a mood. You can review it, deploy it, and hand over the repository.

Pay for the launch against that list. Change the list in writing when the list is wrong. Do not change it by accumulation, with every new idea becoming a quiet extra. A fixed project dies when the edge moves every week and the fee does not. If the edge is moving, you do not have a fixed project. You have a retainer wearing the wrong clothes.

## What a fixed launch includes

Include the decisions, the build, the review, and the handoff. Decisions are the sentence, the structure, and the visual system small enough to use: type, color, and the components you will repeat. Build is the site in the tool you agreed, in accounts you own. Review is a set number of rounds on the work in the scope, not an infinite polish on new ideas. Handoff is the files, the repo, the domain, and a note on how to publish.

The client portal is the practical handoff for brand files, docs, and updates. A fixed launch should end with those in a place the team can open, not in a zip file named final. If the only record is a Figma link on a personal account, the launch is not finished.

Include a check you can point at. For a marketing site, that might be the page on a phone, the form arriving in the right inbox, and the obvious paths working. For a shop, a test order. For a product interface, the empty state and the one error you know happens. Leave performance as a named bar when it matters. [Google's Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) give you that bar: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, cumulative layout shift under 0.1. A fixed launch can include "we will measure these on the key page and fix what we caused." It should not include an unnamed promise to be fast.

Leave out the unknown. Support for a tool you have not chosen. Pages for an audience you have not met. A content program. Those are future work. Put them in a sentence at the bottom of the scope so they are visible and declined.

## When a retainer is the right shape

A retainer is right when the thing you are making will still be changing after the first release, and the cost of a new team learning it each time is higher than the cost of keeping a small one. A product interface in its first year. A site whose offer is rewritten as the company learns. A design system that has to absorb new screens.

The retainer should name a capacity, not a mood. A number of days or a number of shipped pieces in a month. A queue the founder can see. A person who already knows the product. The same people means the same people: if the studio rotates a stranger through the retainer every month, you are paying for a fixed project in installments and losing the memory each time.

Use it for a sequence you can predict in type, even if you cannot predict the exact screen. Examples: a new page when a feature ships, a revision of the homepage sentence, a set of empty states, a pass on the mobile nav. If you cannot imagine four weeks of that work, you do not have a retainer. You have a hope that work will appear.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) warns against changing the date on a page to make it look fresh when the substance has not changed. A retainer is the opposite habit. When the product changes, the page changes for real: the sentence, the picture, the path. If nothing changed, leave the date alone and do not invent a refresh to justify the month. The retainer can include a week of no visible launch, spent on the system, only if you can say what got clearer.

## How retainers fail

They fail when there is no queue. The studio asks what to do, the founder is in sales, and the month becomes meetings about the month. Write the queue in the first week, even if item three is rough. A rough item can be replaced. An empty queue becomes a status call.

They fail when the retainer is a substitute for a decision. "We will figure out the offer inside the retainer" can be honest if the work is a series of pages you will test. It is not honest if you wanted a brand program and a product strategy and a site, and you bought four days a month. The capacity has to match the ambiguity. A large ambiguity needs a fixed discovery with an edge, then a retainer if the result is a living product. It does not need an endless small invoice.

They fail when success is "hours used." Hours are a capacity. Success is a page, a component, a sentence in the product that was wrong and is now plain. Review the shipped things. If a month ships nothing a customer can touch, say so and change the queue or pause.

They fail when the contract punishes stopping. A good retainer can end. The product stabilized, or you hired someone, or the fit was wrong. End it with the files and the accounts in your name, the same way a fixed launch ends. A retainer that is hard to leave is a subscription to a tool, and the tool is your own site.

## How fixed projects fail

They fail when the edge was a wish. You signed for a homepage, and the homepage cannot be written because the offer is three offers. The design will make that obvious in week one. Stop and rewrite the scope. Do not decorate the contradiction.

They fail when new ideas are free. A fixed fee with an open backlog teaches everyone to add. The launch moves, the quality drops, and the relationship sours. New ideas go on a list for after the launch, unless you explicitly trade one in-scope item out.

They fail when handoff is an afterthought. The site launches on the studio's accounts, the font is missing, and the person who knew the deploy is on another project. Put the accounts and the repo in the definition of done. A launch you cannot edit is a picture of a launch.

They fail when the fixed scope includes other people's unknown work: your legal review, a photography shoot with no date, a migration from a vendor who will not export. Those are dependencies. Name the date they are due, and name what happens to the launch if they slip. The studio can build around a missing photograph. It cannot invent the photograph and also keep the date, unless the scope said so.

## A way to decide

Answer in one sitting.

1. Can you list the finished pages or screens without using the phrase "and whatever else we need"?
2. Will the offer or the product still be moving every month after launch?
3. Do you want the same people for that movement, and do you have a queue?

If the first answer is yes and the second is no, fix the launch. If the second and third are yes, use a retainer, and still fix the first release so the retainer has something real to change. If the first answer is no, do not buy either shape yet. Write the offer until the edge appears. A contract will not find it for you.

Many teams do both in order. A fixed launch for the site you can describe. A smaller retainer afterward if the first month proves the page will keep changing. The order matters. A retainer with nothing shipped is a conversation. A launch with a clear edge is a site.

The person who keeps that site current might eventually sit inside the company. Hiring them, and knowing when a studio is still the right seat, is the next decision: [in-house designer or a studio](/blog/in-house-designer-or-a-studio).
